title: Kalbelia folk songs and dances
summary: Kalbelia is a living song-and-dance practice of Kalbelia communities in Rajasthan, inscribed by UNESCO. The compass card ties it to place, community, and sources — not a costume souvenir.
body:
Kalbelia refers to songs and dances associated with Kalbelia communities in Rajasthan. UNESCO lists “Kalbelia folk songs and dances of Rajasthan” on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The practice is a performing art: swirling black skirts, rapid footwork, and snake-related imagery appear in popular descriptions, but those visuals are not a license to invent ritual rules or “ancient secrets.”

For a student or traveller in or near Jaipur, Jodhpur, or Pushkar, the useful questions are narrower. Who performs, in what setting, and what has already been documented by UNESCO, the Ministry of Culture, or open scholarship? Stage shows for tourists can be skilled and paid work; they are not automatically the same as community ceremony. If a guide claims a step “always means” a specific myth, ask for a source. This card will not invent that meaning.

Respectful watching means not grabbing dancers for photos, not demanding “more authentic” versions, and not treating the community as an exhibit. If you ask a question this app cannot retrieve from the card and its cited pages, the answer is that we do not know — not a generated folk tale.

Kalbelia sits in a place–practice graph: Rajasthan as region, performing type, UNESCO badge with an outbound link. GI crafts of the same state (for example Jaipur blue pottery) are neighbours in the explorer, not the same item. A short quiz after this card only tests facts written here and in the listed sources.
calendar_note: Performed year-round; often visible around tourist seasons and local fairs in Rajasthan. Do not treat hotel shows as the only authentic context.

title: Durga Puja in Kolkata
summary: Neighbourhood-scale festival in Kolkata combining worship, public art (pandals), and civic gathering. UNESCO inscribed Durga Puja in Kolkata; this card is a learner path, not a temple timetable.
body:
Durga Puja in Kolkata is a public, neighbourhood festival: temporary pavilions (pandals), images of the goddess Durga and her children, processions, food, and late-night walking routes. UNESCO inscribed “Durga Puja in Kolkata” on the Representative List. The Ministry of Culture and Indian Culture Portal discuss Durga Puja among India’s ICH narratives. That does not make this student app an official calendar.

Do / don’t for a first-time visitor, at the level this card can honestly support: do expect crowds and photography rules that vary by pandal committee; don’t assume every image or chant is free to commercialise; don’t invent caste or “secret tantra” explanations. Committee and household practices differ. If you need visarjan timing for a specific ghat, use a local notice, not a language model.

The innovation of Parampara Path is to bind the festival to West Bengal as a region, mark UNESCO, and let you ask only questions the retrieved text can answer. Quizzes are generated from this card, not from rumours. Contributions (a family memory of a particular para) stay unpublished until a human reviewer accepts them.

Patachitra and other Bengal crafts appear as separate items so the explorer does not collapse “Bengal culture” into one page.
calendar_note: Sharadiya / autumn (Ashwin). Exact city dates follow the Bengali calendar each year — store as season, not a fake Gregorian timestamp.

title: Garba of Gujarat
summary: Garba is a participatory dance-and-song practice of Gujarat, inscribed by UNESCO in 2023. The card separates living practice from club remix culture without shaming either.
body:
Garba of Gujarat is a community dance traditionally associated with Navaratri, circling a lamp or image, with clapping patterns and songs. UNESCO inscribed Garba of Gujarat on the Representative List (2023). Variants exist across districts and in diaspora halls. This card will not publish a “one true choreography.”

A traveller in Ahmedabad or Vadodara during Navaratri may find municipal and neighbourhood events. Dress codes and gender mixing rules are local, not universal. Do not treat film choreography as ethnography. If you ask whether a specific mudra is mandatory, and it is not in the sources below, the system refuses.

Ajrakh and other Gujarati crafts are separate nodes. The compass job is: region Gujarat → Garba card → grounded Q&A → quiz. Social reels of Garba are out of MVP on purpose: they explode moderation risk.
calendar_note: Navaratri (approx. September–October). Regional and diaspora events exist; do not invent a single “correct” step list.

title: Yoga
summary: Yoga is inscribed by UNESCO as an ICH element of India. This card is a source-attributed orientation, not a medical or guru-endorsement product.
body:
Yoga appears on UNESCO’s Representative List as an Indian ICH element. The Ministry of Culture discusses yoga among living heritage narratives. Parampara Path places a learner card in the Uttarakhand / Himalayan foothills node because Rishikesh is a commonly searched place for practice — that is a navigation convenience, not a claim that yoga “belongs only” to one town.

What this card will not do: prescribe asanas for injury, certify teachers, or generate Sanskrit translations of closed lineages. If a question is medical, refuse. If a question is historical and not in the cited pages, refuse.

The product principle is attribution before animation. A quiz tests whether you noticed UNESCO listing and the unofficial-learner stance, not whether you can perform a headstand.

Related items (Vedic chanting, Kumbh) are neighbours in the knowledge/festival graph, not substitutes.
calendar_note: International Day of Yoga is 21 June (UN). Living practice is year-round; studio marketing is not ICH law.

title: Kumbh Mela
summary: Kumbh Mela is a large cyclical pilgrimage gathering inscribed by UNESCO. This card orients learners; it is not crowd-control or ticketing software.
body:
Kumbh Mela is among India’s UNESCO-listed ICH elements: a massive, cyclical gathering of pilgrims, akharas, and temporary cities at rotating river sites. Host geography includes cities in Uttar Pradesh and other states depending on the cycle. This MVP pins a region node to Uttar Pradesh for discoverability (Prayagraj is a widely searched host) while stating clearly that the phenomenon is not “UP-only property.”

Safety, stamps, and exact bathing minutes are operational matters for authorities. This app must not hallucinate them. Ask may refuse crowd numbers that are not in the card. Contributions about family pilgrimage stay in a pending queue.

Do not depict restricted initiatory knowledge. Public festival description is enough for a student MVP.
calendar_note: Cycle of gatherings at rotating host cities; dates follow traditional calendars. Do not invent the next snan minute.

title: Kutiyattam, Sanskrit theatre
summary: Kutiyattam is a Sanskrit theatre tradition of Kerala inscribed by UNESCO. Treat it as a specialist performing lineage, not a tourist skit generator.
body:
Kutiyattam (Koodiyattam) is a form of Sanskrit theatre practised in Kerala, with UNESCO inscription on the Representative List. Training, gesture vocabularies, and temple associations are specialised. This card will not generate a fake scene-by-scene script or claim that every Kerala tourist show is Kutiyattam.

For learners: use outbound UNESCO and MoC pages; respect that some performance contexts are not drop-in tourist products. Ask refuses costume “meanings” that are not in sources. Related Kerala nodes include Mudiyettu and Onam, which are different practices.
calendar_note: Temple and stage calendars vary; do not invent show times.

title: Chhau dance
summary: Chhau is a masked or martial-inflected dance family spanning Odisha, Jharkhand, and West Bengal. MoC notes vulnerability to falling participation.
body:
Chhau dance is UNESCO-listed. Styles associated with Seraikella, Purulia, and Mayurbhanj are often distinguished in public literature; this card will not invent a fourth “official” national style. The Ministry of Culture has described Chhau as pressured by modern influences and declining participation — a reminder that living heritage is not guaranteed.

Odisha is the region pin for discovery; neighbouring states also host styles. Masks and martial vocabulary are documented at a high level; sacred or closed details are omitted. Do not use Ask to generate a combat manual.
calendar_note: Seasonal and community performance calendars vary across Seraikella, Purulia, and Mayurbhanj styles.

title: Sankirtana of Manipur
summary: Sankirtana is a ritual singing-and-drumming practice of Manipur inscribed by UNESCO.
body:
Sankirtana (Manipur) is a UNESCO-listed performing/ritual singing practice with drums and dance in Vaishnava contexts as described on official ICH pages. This learner card will not reconstruct full liturgy, nor treat it as a nightclub genre.

Ask refuses unsourced claims about caste or “secret” verses. Contributions of family attendance memories are allowed as pending text, not as theology.
calendar_note: Temple and festival contexts; do not invent liturgy.

title: Thathera metal craft of Jandiala Guru
summary: Traditional brass and copper utensil making of the Thatheras of Jandiala Guru, Punjab — UNESCO listed and a craft-economy story, not a souvenir mill.
body:
The traditional brass and copper craft of the Thatheras of Jandiala Guru is a UNESCO-listed ICH element. Public descriptions emphasise hammered utensils and a specialised artisan community in Punjab. GI and craft-economy writing in India often treats metalware as livelihood plus authenticity — still poorly explained to youth, which is this product’s gap.

This card will not set prices, certify GI labels for a stall, or generate a metallurgy textbook. If you are at a fair, the learner job is: name, place, UNESCO pointer, and how-it-is-made at summary level. Phulkari is a neighbouring Punjab textile practice, not the same item.

Photos: prefer own or clearly licensed images later; captions must not imply Ministry ownership of this app.
calendar_note: Workshop practice is ongoing; not a one-day festival.

title: Ramman, religious festival and ritual theatre of the Garhwal Himalayas
summary: Ramman is a UNESCO-listed religious festival and ritual theatre of Garhwal.
body: Ramman combines festival and ritual theatre in the Garhwal Himalayas and is UNESCO-listed. It is place-specific. This card will not relocate it to a generic “hill station package.” Closed or highly local ritual details stay out. Yoga and Ramman share a region node but are different types.
calendar_note: Village festival cycle in Garhwal; do not invent the next date.

title: Ramlila, traditional performance of the Ramayana
summary: Ramlila is a traditional performance of the Ramayana, UNESCO-listed, with many local forms.
body: Ramlila is UNESCO-listed as traditional performance of the Ramayana. Forms differ by town. This card refuses a single national script dump and refuses to adjudicate sectarian disputes. UP is a discovery pin because many well-known Ramlilas are discussed there; performances exist elsewhere. Durga Puja and Ramlila are different festival/theatre complexes.
calendar_note: Often around Dussehra; local calendars vary widely.
quiz_title: Ramlila, traditional performance of the Ramayana — checks

title: Mudiyettu
summary: Mudiyettu is a ritual theatre of Kerala inscribed by UNESCO. Tourist packaging is not the same as temple permission.
body: Mudiyettu is UNESCO-listed ritual theatre in Kerala. This card describes it at a public ICH level only. Do not autoplay chanting. Do not generate a how-to for costume or possession. Kutiyattam is a related but distinct Kerala performing lineage.
calendar_note: Bhagavati / temple-related ritual theatre calendar; omit restricted practice details.

title: Tradition of Vedic chanting
summary: UNESCO lists the tradition of Vedic chanting. This card will not dump copyrighted recitations or closed-school secrets.
body: The tradition of Vedic chanting is a UNESCO-listed oral heritage. Transmission is specialised. This MVP will not host full recitation audio, autoplay mantras, or claim to replace a teacher. The UP pin is a weak geographic convenience for the explorer, not a statement that chanting exists only there. Ask refuses to “translate secretly” unsourced verses.
calendar_note: Living oral transmission; not a playlist product.

title: Buddhist chanting of Ladakh
summary: UNESCO lists Buddhist chanting of Ladakh. Treat monasteries as living communities, not film sets.
body: Buddhist chanting of Ladakh is UNESCO-listed. Learners should expect that recording rules are local. This card will not generate a “secret tantra tourist pack.” Ask refuses unsourced claims about specific rites. Related: Yoga is a different knowledge item.
calendar_note: Monastic calendars; visitor access is not guaranteed.

title: Deepavali
summary: Deepavali was inscribed by UNESCO in 2025. This card stresses regional variation and refuses a single pan-India ritual script.
body:
Deepavali (Diwali) is listed on UNESCO’s India ICH page as an inscribed element (2025 inscription referenced in the research brief). Practices differ by region: lamps, Lakshmi puja, new year associations, Jain and Sikh observances, and local foodways. Tamil Nadu is a discovery pin, not exclusive ownership.

This card will not generate fireworks safety law for every municipal ward, nor a shopping list. Ask may refuse “what does every Hindu must do.” Pongal is a separate Tamil festival item. Kanchipuram silk may appear in gift economies but is a craft node, not the festival itself.
calendar_note: Lunar calendar; national public holiday dates are announced annually. Regional names and emphases differ (Deepavali / Diwali).

title: Jaipur blue pottery
summary: Blue-glazed pottery associated with Jaipur — a GI craft learner card, not a shop.
body:
Jaipur blue pottery is a distinctive glazed ceramic practice associated with Jaipur, often discussed in GI and handicraft narratives. Quartz-based bodies and turquoise-blue palettes appear in public craft writing. This card will not certify a stall’s GI status or invent a Mughal origin story beyond what sources support.

At a mela, the job-to-be-done is name, region, GI-as-authenticity-frame, and making-at-summary-level. Kalbelia is a performing neighbour in Rajasthan, not a glaze recipe. Payments and marketplaces are out of MVP.
calendar_note: Workshop / market calendars vary.

title: Banarasi brocade weaving

body: Banarasi weaving is widely discussed as a GI-tagged silk/brocade tradition of Varanasi. This card explains place and craft at summary level. It will not set gold-zari prices or generate caste commentary. Ramlila and Kumbh share the UP node as different types. Do not scrape full commercial catalogues.

title: Channapatna lacquer toys

body: Channapatna toys are lacquered wooden toys associated with a Karnataka GI craft cluster. Vegetable dyes and turning techniques appear in public craft explainers. This card will not claim EN-71 lab results. Mysore inlay is a separate Karnataka craft. Native apps and 3D toys are out of MVP.

title: Kanchipuram silk weaving
summary: Temple-town silk weaving associated with Kanchipuram, framed for learners not couture checkout.
body: Kanchipuram silk is a GI-associated weaving tradition of Tamil Nadu. Contrast borders and temple-town identity appear in public writing. This card will not authenticate a sari label. Deepavali and Pongal are festival neighbours. No marketplace.

title: Bidriware
summary: Zinc-alloy inlay metalware associated with Bidar/Hyderabad Deccan GI narratives.
body: Bidriware is a dark metal inlay craft of the Deccan, often GI-tagged in craft mapping. Silver inlay on a darkened alloy is the public visual signature. This card will not reconstruct a full chemical recipe. Telangana is the pin; historical Bidar geography is acknowledged as wider than one modern state label. Thathera is a different metal story in Punjab.
calendar_note: Workshop / market calendars vary.

title: Madhubani / Mithila painting
summary: Wall and paper painting of the Mithila region — GI craft, not an NFT drop.
body: Madhubani (Mithila) painting is a well-known Bihar GI/art practice: ritual wall painting that also exists on paper for wider markets. Motifs and gender of traditional practitioners are often discussed in public arts writing; this card will not exoticise communities. No comments-as-forum. Contributions of family wall-painting memories stay pending.
calendar_note: Workshop / market calendars vary.

title: Warli painting
summary: Warli painting of Maharashtra — living graphic language, not a generic “tribal sticker pack.”
body: Warli painting is associated with Warli communities in Maharashtra, with public-domain-adjacent visual tropes (white on earth grounds) that are often misused in design. This card names the community as sources do and refuses “exotic tribe” copy. Ganesh Utsav is a separate festival node. Ask refuses unsourced claims about sacred images you may not reproduce.
calendar_note: Workshop / market calendars vary.

title: Pattachitra
summary: Cloth/palm-leaf painting traditions of Odisha (and related Bengal pata), framed carefully as living craft.
body: Pattachitra refers to painting on cloth (and related pata traditions) associated especially with Odisha in GI conversations, with Bengal pata as a related but not identical practice. This card will not collapse them. Chhau is a performing neighbour in Odisha. Copyright: do not paste entire illustrated manuscripts.

title: Lucknow Chikankari
summary: White-on-white embroidery associated with Lucknow — GI craft learner card.
body: Chikankari is an embroidery practice associated with Lucknow, often GI-tagged. This card stays at summary making-level. It will not rank workshops. Banarasi weaving is a different UP textile. No checkout.

title: Kalamkari

title: Dhokra / bell-metal casting
summary: Lost-wax bell-metal casting associated with central Indian craft belts including Chhattisgarh.
body: Dhokra (lost-wax metal casting) is discussed across central and eastern India. This MVP uses a Chhattisgarh pin as a discovery default and states that related practices exist in neighbouring states. It will not dump a foundry safety manual. Bidri and Thathera are different metal systems.

title: Phulkari embroidery
summary: Floral embroidery of Punjab — GI textile, distinct from Thathera metalcraft.
body: Phulkari is a Punjab embroidery tradition often present in GI maps. This card stays with public descriptions of darn-stitch floral fields. It will not dictate wedding custom law. Thathera is the UNESCO metal neighbour in Punjab.

title: Kashmir Pashmina

body: Pashmina is a Kashmir GI/authenticity story in craft writing. This card will not run a fibre lab or invent a microscopic test. It will not collapse politics into a shopping slogan. Ask refuses unsourced “always 100%” claims for a specific stall.

summary: Painted wooden toys of Kondapalli, Andhra Pradesh.
body: Kondapalli toys are a painted wood-toy GI cluster in Andhra Pradesh. Distinct from Channapatna lacquer. This card will not invent EN test IDs. Kalamkari is a textile neighbour.

title: Ajrakh printing
summary: Resist-dyed block printing associated with Kutch / Sindh-Kutch corridors.
body: Ajrakh is a block-printed, resist-dyed textile practice associated with Kutch (and a wider Thar–Sindh world). This card uses a Gujarat pin and notes cross-border historical geography without turning into foreign-policy content. Garba is a festival neighbour. Natural-dye chemistry is summary-level only.

title: Muga silk of Assam
summary: Golden Muga silk of Assam — GI craft beside Bihu, not a checkout flow.
body: Muga silk is an Assam GI identity craft: a golden silk from Antheraea assamensis in public science/craft writing. This card will not run a sericulture course. Bihu is the festival neighbour. No marketplace.

title: Onam
summary: Harvest / Malayali new year festival of Kerala with public and household forms.
body: Onam is a major Kerala festival with pookalam, sadya, and public events. It is not UNESCO-listed on this card. Kutiyattam and Mudiyettu are different Kerala practices. This card will not invent a single “authentic sadya menu” for every household. Ask refuses unsourced caste jokes.
calendar_note: Chingam (Malayalam calendar); national/regional holiday dates vary by year.

title: Bihu
summary: Assamese seasonal festival cycle with dance, music, and community gathering.
body: Bihu refers to a set of Assamese seasonal festivals, of which Bohag Bihu is the most widely known nationally. This card will not collapse all three into one Bollywood number. Muga silk is a craft neighbour. Ask refuses unsourced claims about “the only real Bihu district.”
calendar_note: Three Bihus in the agricultural year (Bohag, Kati, Magh) — seasonal, not a fake timestamp.

title: Pongal
summary: Tamil harvest festival, distinct from Deepavali.
body: Pongal is a Tamil harvest festival with multi-day household practices. Deepavali is a separate festival card. Kanchipuram silk is a craft neighbour. This card will not generate a fire-safety code for sugarcane burning in every village.
calendar_note: Thai month (mid-January in many public calendars); multi-day household and community forms.

title: Ganesh Utsav
summary: Public Ganesha festival especially associated with Maharashtra cities.
body: Ganesh Utsav / Ganesh Chaturthi is a major public festival in Maharashtra with household and mandal forms. Sahapedia Map’s city mapping is a related research neighbour, not something we scrape wholesale. Warli is a craft neighbour. Exact visarjan minutes are local notices, not RAG fiction.
calendar_note: Bhadrapada; visarjan days are local. Do not invent a ghat minute.

title: Theyyam
summary: Ritual performance of northern Kerala. Public ICH-level description only; no how-to.
body: Theyyam is a ritual performance tradition of northern Kerala, often discussed in open heritage writing. This card uses type=ritual, omits restricted knowledge, and will not generate possession manuals. Photography ethics are local. Kutiyattam and Mudiyettu are different Kerala items. Autoplay audio is forbidden.
calendar_note: Shrine season in northern Kerala; access and photography rules are local.

title: Nawrouz (Parsi New Year in Indian cities)
summary: Nowruz is a UNESCO-listed multinational element; this card only orients Indian Parsi civic observance at summary level.
body: Nawrouz/Nowruz is on UNESCO’s lists as a shared multinational heritage. This student card does not claim India owns it. It only orients learners to Parsi community new-year observance in Indian cities (Mumbai pin as discovery). It will not adjudicate calendar sects. Inventing a single “correct Indian Nowruz date” is refused.
calendar_note: March equinox period for many Nowruz observances; Parsi Jamshedi Navroz follows the Shahenshahi calendar — do not fake a single date.

title: Kangra painting
summary: Pahari miniature painting associated with Kangra, Himachal Pradesh.
body: Kangra painting is a Pahari miniature tradition discussed in GI and museum writing. This card will not dump entire collections or generate fake accession numbers. It is a hill-region craft/knowledge of making, not a replacement for IGNCA. Photography of living ritual is not implied.

title: Khurja pottery
summary: Ceramic cluster of Khurja, Uttar Pradesh — GI craft distinct from Jaipur blue pottery.
body: Khurja pottery is a large ceramic cluster in Uttar Pradesh, often GI-mapped. Distinct from Jaipur blue pottery (different body, glaze, and place). This card will not invent lead-test certificates. Banarasi weaving and Chikankari are textile neighbours in UP, not ceramics.
